For weeks, a group in Chinmay's class had been calling him "zero" and moving their chairs when he sat down. By now he believed it: nobody at school wanted him. He spent every lunch break hiding in the library, pretending to read.
On Thursday, Usha Ma'am, the librarian, sat opposite him. "You're here every single day. Is something going on?"
Chinmay's throat closed. Then, very quietly, he said it aloud: "Nobody wants me around."
Usha Ma'am listened to all of it. "That's what they want you to believe. It isn't true." She told his class teacher before the last bell, and then showed him the notice for the library quiz club. "They meet here on Fridays. I think you'd fit."

qa.q: Where did Chinmay spend every lunch break?
qa.a: In the library, pretending to read.

qa.q: What did Chinmay believe about himself because of the bullying?
qa.a: He felt lonely and unwanted, believing nobody at school wanted him around.

qa.q: How did saying it aloud to Usha Ma'am help?
qa.a: It broke the secrecy: she told him the belief wasn't true, informed his class teacher that day and pointed him to a club where he could fit.

qa.q: How might Usha Ma'am have seen Chinmay before he spoke?
qa.a: Usha Ma'am noticed he was there every day and suspected something was wrong, which is why she sat down and asked.

grounding: A bullied boy comes to believe nobody wants him; saying it aloud to a librarian breaks the secrecy and points him to a club where he fits.

I'm Harish, and I still remember the night the class group chat went off. Someone had posted a photo of me at sports day, falling face-first into the long-jump pit. Under it: laughing faces, one after another. "Sand monster lol."
My hands shook. I started typing something furious, then stopped. Instead I took screenshots, like my cousin had once told me, and went to Appa.
He read every message. "None of this is on you, and we can stop it." He saved the screenshots and messaged the class teacher that night. The photo was gone by morning.
Later, Anand messaged me privately: "I didn't laugh. That was mean." I read it three times.

qa.q: What was the photo in the class group chat?
qa.a: A photo of Harish falling face-first into the long-jump pit at sports day.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when the laughing faces kept appearing?
qa.a: Harish felt humiliated and angry, with shaking hands and the urge to type something furious.

qa.q: Why was saving screenshots and going to Appa a wise choice?
qa.a: It kept proof and brought in an adult, so the class teacher was told that night and the photo was removed by morning.

qa.q: How might Anand feel about what happened in the chat?
qa.a: Anand seems uncomfortable with the mocking and wants Harish to know not everyone laughed.

grounding: Classmates laugh at an embarrassing photo in the class group chat; the child does not reply in anger, saves screenshots and tells a parent, and it is stopped.

This morning Gurleen came to me before assembly with her mother's phone. The night before, Ramesh had posted a photo of her asleep on the bus during the school trip, mouth open. Twenty classmates had reacted with laughing faces.

Tuesday. At home, Naveen practised in the mirror with Amma. "Stop that. I don't like it." At first his voice wobbled. By the tenth try, it was calm and firm, and he stood taller.

passage:
At the swimming club, Lalit liked calling Pranav "the drowning fish" whenever Pranav paused at the shallow end. The other boys snorted. It felt like a joke.
On Saturday, Lalit walked up behind him in the changing room. Pranav jumped and pressed himself against the lockers, eyes wide.
Lalit stopped. He had meant to say something funny. Instead a cold feeling crept up his neck. Pranav was scared of him. Not laughing. Scared.
After practice, Lalit found him by the vending corner. "Pranav, I'm sorry. For the fish thing. All of it. I'll stop." He meant it.
Pranav nodded slowly. The next Saturday, nobody called him a fish.

qa.q: What did Lalit call Pranav at the swimming club?
qa.a: "The drowning fish".

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when Pranav pressed against the lockers?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and shaken, a cold feeling creeping up his neck as he realised Pranav was scared of him.

qa.q: Why was Lalit's apology better than calling it a joke?
qa.a: He saw the fear was real, said sorry and meant it, and then actually stopped, which ended the hurt.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Lalit coming up behind him?
qa.a: Pranav sees him as a threat, jumping and pressing himself against the lockers.

grounding: A boy sees the boy he teases flinch in fear; instead of feeling proud he feels uncomfortable, stops and apologises sincerely.
